articles.text: The Exedra, with its Blue Vase, is the most iconic place in Piedmont. Iron gates lead from Magnolia and Highland Avenues to Exedra Plaza, flanked by a group of 10 Highland Poplars. These stately oval Poplars were designated as Heritage Trees in 2018 upon the nomination of Jim Horner. They offer shade to park goers and enhance the beauty of Exedra Plaza year-round. Highland Poplars are cotton-less cottonwood trees that are fast growing and adaptable. They are drought tolerant, disease resistant, unbothered by urban pollution, and not particular to any soil type. They are shady deciduous trees with large heartshaped leaves that turn a lovely yellow in the fall. Highland Poplars can be expected to grow 50 feet tall and require only occasional maintenance. This hybrid species was propagated by a nursery in Colorado. It is just a happy coincidence that they found a home along Highland Avenue in Piedmont. articles.text: Like many others, our family wanted to add our gratitude regarding the return to in-person classes for K through 6th grades at Piedmont schools and its plans to return all other grades. Although in-person hours remain extremely limited, the impact has been immediate and incredibly positive. Thank you to all who have worked so hard to make this happen, especially our teachers and staff. We also thank PUSD for taking an important first step to address its past lack of transparency and communication failures with the new Piedmont Ahead. Piedmonters should visit this website regularly, as it often includes important details that may not be mentioned in the weekly PUSD emails sent to district parents. This week a timely “Question of the Week” was included – What is the district doing to plan for fall re-opening? In its answer, the District announced that it is developing plans for the 2021/2022 school year based on five different scenarios, which range from full-time in-person to full-time distant learning. In particular, two articulated scenarios allow for in-person schooling, while requiring adherence to social distancing of 4 feet (per current CDC guidelines and as currently allowed by Alameda County), or 6 feet (as currently required under MOUs with the PUSD unions, which are set to expire this June). The difference of two feet could create significant hurdles to accomplishing a return to fulltime in-person learning, especially for Piedmont Middle School, given its space constraints. We would strongly encourage all concerned parents to attend the March 24th School Board meeting to better understand how the Board and superintendent intend to advocate for Piedmonters, students, faculty and staff. We will be speaking up in support of finding creative solutions to guarantee a return to full-time in-person learning in the Fall. It is our hope that Mr. Booker and the Board will bring a level of leadership, transparency and creativity so that, as a community, we can rise to the challenge. Together, we can find a way to return safely to full-time in-person learning this fall. Our children deserve nothing less.
articles.title: Two-feet could make all the difference

articles.text: The late Eugene Peterson was one of the great pastors and biblical interpreters of our time. He is best known for The Message, a very popular translation of the New Testament into contemporary English. This is the way he translates the story of the healing of Simon Peter’s mother-in law in the Gospel of Mark. Directly on leaving the meeting place, they came to Simon and Andrew’s house, accompanied by James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law was sick in bed, burning up with fever. They told Jesus. He went to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up. No sooner had the fever left than she was up fixing dinner for them. I would not challenge Peterson’s translation. He is a scholar of impeccable credentials. However, I would suggest, especially in the midst of Women’s History Month, that “she was up fixing them dinner” is not the only way to read the passage. The word all the gospel writers use for the service Peter’s motherin-law provides is an important one. It is diekonei. It can mean all kinds of service, help and ministry. It is worth noting that when the New Testament writers describe what church leaders do, they often use the root word diakonia. I don’t think it is far-fetched to say that the healed woman ministered to Jesus and his community of followers. I don’t think it is far-fetched to suggest that the ministry she provided may have looked a lot like communion, even before there was a well-established tradition of communion. Starting next week, healthcare providers can vaccinate individuals ages 16 to 64 with certain health conditions that leaves them more at risk to COVID-19 mortality. The bulletin directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. This new group of eligible residents will join thousands of other people who can get vaccinated in Alameda County. The initial group that could get vaccinated back in December is called Phase 1A and includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group includes an estimated 145,000 people in the county. Last month, Phase 1B became eligible. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. articles.text: Editor: The old Piedmont pool served our community nearly sixty years. It can be hoped that the new pool will serve us just as long – until at least the year 2080. But what will the world be like in 2080? In particular, how will we be getting our energy, and how can the pool we build now anticipate this changed energy world? A pool facility that simply continues to heat and power itself with fossil fuel, as the old pool did, is out of line with the changes we must make to our energy sources to combat the most devastating effects of climate change. Both the State of California and the City of Piedmont have committed to reducing their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to 80% or more below 1990 levels by 2050, with an interim target of 40% below 1990 levels by 2030. As our community begins to reflect on how to design the new pool, we need to consider how to minimize its GHG emissions. A main decarbonization strategy in California is to electrify all appliances that currently run on natural gas, which is a fossil fuel (despite the gloss the gas industry tries to put on it). Using electric heat pumps and other green technologies instead of natural gas to warm the pool would eliminate the pool’s GHG emissions from natural gas usage; and, as California’s electricity mix moves towards California’s 2045 goal of it being 100% from renewable sources, GHG emissions associated with the facility’s electrical use would decrease over time, giving us a carbon neutral pool by 2050. We could perhaps get to carbon neutral even sooner by generating some of our own electricity from renewable sources (for example, solar). At present, there are no cookie cutter models for designing an all-electric public pool, but we know of at least one other city (Mountain View) that is currently trying. With all the can-do energy, talent, and resources of the Piedmont community, we believe we can take on this challenge of designing and building an all-electric, energy-efficient pool, serving as a role model for other cities across the state and nation. -Indira Balkissoon Amy Griffith Garrett Keating Marianne Mitosinka Margaret Ovenden Tom Webster For 22 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The bulletin directs healthcare providers to “use their clinical judgement” to vaccinate people “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk for morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 as a direct result of one or more of the severe health conditions.” The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found with the state’s guidance at the California Department of Public Health’s website at www.cdph.ca.gov. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments. This new group of eligible residents will join thousands of other people who can get vaccinated in Alameda County. The initial group that could get vaccinated back in December is called Phase 1A and includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. This group includes an estimated 145,000 people in the county. Last month, Phase 1B became eligible. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. Phase 1B numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. After these two phases and people with comorbidities, the county is moving to an age-based priority framework in determining vaccine eligibility. It can be hoped that the new pool will serve us just as long – until at least the year 2080. But what will the world be like in 2080? In particular, how will we be getting our energy, and how can the pool we build now anticipate this changed energy world? A pool facility that simply continues to heat and power itself with fossil fuel, as the old pool did, is out of line with the changes we must make to our energy sources to combat the most devastating effects of climate change. Both the State of California and the City of Piedmont have committed to reducing their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to 80% or more below 1990 levels by 2050, with an interim target of 40% below 1990 levels by 2030. As our community begins to reflect on how to design the new pool, we need to consider how to minimize its GHG emissions. A main decarbonization strategy in California is to electrify all appliances that currently run on natural gas, which is a fossil fuel (despite the gloss the gas industry tries to put on it). Using electric heat pumps and other green technologies instead of natural gas to warm the pool would eliminate the pool’s GHG emissions from natural gas usage; and, as California’s electricity mix moves towards California’s 2045 goal of it being 100% from renewable sources, GHG emissions associated with the facility’s electrical use would decrease over time, giving us a carbon neutral pool by 2050. We could perhaps get to carbon neutral even sooner by generating some of our own electricity from renewable sources (for example, solar). At present, there are no cookie cutter models for designing an all-electric public pool, but we know of at least one other city (Mountain View) that is currently trying. articles.text: Last year there was a lot of attention on the Black experience in America, and one topic that must be included in that discussion is the impact of Black climate activists. Research shows that climate change does not impact all populations equally, and that Black communities face the negative effects of climate change more often than others. Due to this unequal burden, there is a long and important history of Black Americans leading the way on climate crises. This disparity can be seen in obvious ways, such as the infamous Flint, Michigan water and public health crisis, which impacted tens of thousands of people. Flint has a population that is over 50 percent African American, and the crises’ impacts on the community will be felt for decades. Another example is the Hurricane Katrina disaster, which killed over 1,000 people in New Orleans, a city which is 60 percent African-American. After Katrina, Black homeowners received $8,000 less in government aid than white homeowners because of housing value disparities. Predominantly black communities are more likely to be adjacent to landfills, hazardous waste sites, and industrial facilities. Black Americans are 40 percent more likely to have asthma than White Americans. These health outcomes are a direct effect of policy decisions that perpetuate unequal outcomes for different races in America. These health outcomes can be seen close to home. Oakland, which is 64 percent non-White, has childhood asthma rates of 18.3 percent. Compare this to Piedmont, which is approximately 75 percent white, and has child asthma rates of 12 percent. While mere miles apart, the discrepancies are vast. Black Americans, and particularly Black women, have been at the forefront of movements to make the environment a more equitable place to live for all. A local example is the Black Panther movement in Oakland which has organized drives to keep predominantly Black neighborhoods free of waste, host free health clinics, and educate communities on the dangers of pollution. Now, there are numerous groups in Oakland, throughout the Bay Area, and the state, that are focused on environmental issues, often helmed by Black people. One of these groups include the Climate Action Coalition located in Oakland. The Coalition works on numerous issues such as transit, food justice, and adaptation to climate change. Their overarching mission is racial and economic justice, which is directly related to climate solutions. Another group, Communities for a Better Environment, works in low-income Latino and African-American communities in Richmond and Oakland to address health hazards in these communities. Their overarching goal is to prevent and reduce pollution and build healthy communities and environment. The California Environmental Justice Coalition (CEJC) is led by people of color and low-income communities. CEJC follows the principles of environmental justice and is committed to environmental, social, and economic justice. Request a Virtual or On-Site Quote

articles.text: The city of Piedmont is seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA 6) Planning Period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. The City Council unanimously approved the proposal at its meeting on March 2, and a Requests for Proposal [RFP] was issued the following day. The City’s current Housing Element of the General Plan was adopted in 2011 and outlines the city’s housing goals from 2015 to 2023. The State of California requires that each jurisdiction’s housing element be updated every eight years and certified by the State. While most portions of a General Plan are updated every 20 to 25 years, State law requires that the Housing Element be updated in 8-year cycles. Piedmont will begin updating its Housing Element for the 2023- 2031 period, and a major component of this update is the 6th Cycle Regional Housing Needs Assessment (“RHNA”), in which the State estimates each region’s housing needs for all income groups. Piedmont expects an RHNA 6th cycle of approximately 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in RHNA 5th cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units. To ensure that the city meets its housing needs assessment, it will seek a consulting firm. Barry Miller, Principal of Barry Miller Consulting, prepared the city’s documents for the last three cycles, but is not available this year. While the firm selected will be asked to address a number of important housing issues, the most significant work effort is expected to be meeting the RHNA numbers in this upcoming cycle, according to City Administrator Sara Lillevand. Submission of the next cycle’s adopted Housing Element is due to the State by January 2023. To meet this requirement, the city is listing Summer 2021 as a tentative due date for any RHNA appeals, and the first review of the draft housing element to take place in Summer 2022. The RFP was issued on March 3, and proposals are due by April 5. The City Council consideration of the contract is expected to be May 3.
articles.title: City seeks consulting firm to assist with next Housing element cycle

My boys use gaming as their only way of connecting with friends, so I say yes because I know they are lonely and miss their friends, but if the boys are on, my daughter wants to be on...and the cycle continues. So, here are five totally wacky ideas to get kids off screen, even if it’s for just a few extra minutes. 1. Ipad Scavenger Hunt Hide the ipad. Yes, for real, hide it really well. Then create a series of clues directing your kids all over the house or backyard – or both – in order to find it. articles.text: With happy kids coming home from school again, it feels like a new day in town. We thank every support staff member, teacher, administrator, and school board member for getting our kids back in the classroom. It’s heartwarming and a relief, but we must say—we’re already worried about school in the fall. On Monday night, Berkeley Unified School District announced their elementary schools would start full-time instruction on March 29. Other Bay Area districts now plan to open full-time this spring for all grades. Meanwhile, PUSD and the school board say the current schedule is all we can count on. For Piedmont Middle School, that’s two and a half hours at school once a week. Most of the school board say it’s their intention and hope to bring back students full-time this fall, but they can’t possibly commit due to outside circumstances. “Hope” and “intention” are not strategies that will bring PUSD students back full time. We’re told it’s difficult for Piedmont teachers and administrators to be out of step with their fellow Alameda County unions and districts. We say shouldn’t Piedmont lead by example, showing a possible safe return for all students elementary through high school? We’re told it’s difficult for PUSD to plan now when the guidelines may change. We say why not plan with the current set of guidelines? This March, we urge the school board to: • Pass a resolution to open PUSD for full-time in-person instruction to the maximum extent allowable by law for the 2021-2022 school year. • Direct PUSD to plan for full day classroom instruction and to make the shift at the earliest possible date this spring. It’s our understanding that Alameda County does not necessarily require six foot spacing. In June of 2020, almost 800 Piedmont parents, students, and community members signed a petition calling on PUSD to utilize the time, talent, and treasure of Piedmont residents to make space a non-issue. We urge PUSD to end its use of the six foot distancing rule and use all its facilities and other Piedmont public spaces so all students can attend school. We are grateful to all who have worked to get our kids back in the classroom, and to our exceptional teachers for continuing the great education they provide. We also thank the parents for helping create a Covid testing program for students, raising funds for air purifiers, and providing masks for the district. We aren’t enemies. We’re great partners. Let’s continue to work together. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is calling for volunteers to serve on City commissions and committees. Currently, a total of 19 positions will become available. Of the vacancies opening up, 12 are guaranteed to be available. The remaining positions potentially will be filled by incumbents. How to Apply Residents interested in volunteering may fill out and submit an application form on the city’s website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notifications/commission___committee_volunteers_sought_2021. Applications are due to City Hall by March 17 and may be sent by e-mail to the City Clerk’s office (JTulloch@piedmont. ca.gov), or delivered in person to Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The deadline is 5 p.m. on March 17. Applicants must be available for an interview with the City Council on the evenings of Monday, March 22 or March 29. Appointments may be made on March 29. For more information or to request an application to be mailed, call the City Clerk at 420- 3040. The commissions and committees with at least one guaranteed opening that will not be filled by an incumbent include the CIP Review Committee, Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, Civil Service Committee, Public Safety Committee, and Recreation Commission. The Housing Advisory Committee is a newly formed committee with no current or previous members. Vacancies also exist on the following commissions and committees, but these spots may be filled by incumbents: Park Commission, Planning Commission, Police & Fire Pension Board & City Investment Subcommittee. Historically, incumbents who wish to continue their service sign up for a second term. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee 2 vacancies; 3-year term Reviews and provides comment on five year projections contained in the City’s annual budget proposal, the proposed funding and expenditures from several long-term funds, and the proposed mid-year budget adjustments; Provides a financial review of new programs in excess of $250,000 per year. The committee includes Cathie Geddeis, Deborah Leland, Christina Paul, Maya Rath, Frank Ryan, and Chris Kwei as Alternate. Bill Hosler, the long-time chair, will term out. Civic Improvement Projects (CIP) Review Committee 2 vacancies, 3-year term The committee makes recommendations to the City Council regarding the expenditure of the capital budget (construction, repair or rehabilitation of city facilities). The committee meets as required. Committee members include John Lenahan, Chair, Bobbe Stehr, and Michael Henn, Sue Herrick will term out. Civil Service Commission 1 vacancy, 2 incumbents; 3-year term The commission deals with personnel issues including classification and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. This commission meets as required. Members of the commission include Michael Reese, Sandra Rappaport, Scott Lawson, Claudia Harrison, and David Hobstetter. Lawson and Reese are eligible to reapply for another 3-year term. Sandra Rappaport has termed out. Park Commission 2 vacancies; 2 incumbents; 3-year term Makes recommendations to the City Council about improvements to the public parks and manages the street tree improvement program of the city. Meets monthly on the first Wednesday at 5:30 p.m. Members of the commission include Patty Dunlap, Betsy Goodman, Amber Brumfiel, Jim Horner, Brian Mahany, Eileen Ruby, and Robin Wu, Brumfiel and Dunlap, the Commission Chair, are eligible to reapply for a second term. Planning Commission 1 vacancy, 1 incumbents; 3-year term The Planning Commission makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. It advises the City Council on issues related to planning and building. It meets monthly on the second Monday at 5:30 p.m. It requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Appointees to the Planning Commission are required to submit a statement of economic interests. Members include Allison Allessio, Chair, Jonathan Levine, Tom Ramsey, Yildiz Duransoy, Rani Batra, and Douglas Strout as Alternate commissioner. Alessio is eligible for a second term. Public Safety Committee 2 vacancies, 3-year term This committee investigates ways to increase public participation in crime reduction; It increases public participation in disaster preparedness, and provides a forum for residents to share comments, issues or concerns regarding public safety issues. The committee meets quarterly. Committee members include Lynne Wright, Chair, Lori Elefant, Jeffrey Horner, Chris Houlder, and Shanti Brien. Judge Horner is eligible to reapply for a second term. Garrett Keating has termed out. Recreation Commission 2 vacancies, 3-year term The commission advises the City Council on issues regarding the City’s recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space and other issues. It meets monthly on the third Wednesday at 7:30 p.m. Members include Dick Carter, Jeffrey Dorman, and Vincent Fisher. Steve Roland, the commission chair, has termed out. Wednesday, March 10, 2021 11 It's Springtime in Piedmont By Allyson Aleksey Spring doesn’t officially arrive until March 20, but don’t tell that to all the daffodils, tulips and flowering trees throughout Piedmont. It’s early March, and the city is bursting with color – and spring fragrances. The city’s Public Works Department planted approximately 16,000 tulip and daffodil bulbs in November last year. Bulbs were planted around City Hall, the Community Hall, the Exedra Plaza, the Center for the Arts, Civic Center traffic medians, Piedmont Park, Crocker Park, Hampton Park, Dracena Park, the Coaches Field entry, Blair Park, Hall Fenway, Grand Avenue traffic medians, and the traffic triangles at Linda-Kingston, and Hampton-Indian. Some spots are starting to bloom already, but the most visible locations are in Crocker Park and Piedmont Park. And possibly the best is yet to come. The dazzling cherry trees in Piedmont’s Main Park will be blooming soon, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalés. Last night, Tuesday, March 9, playing under the lights at Witter Field in a rainstorm, they beat North Coast Section rival Acalanes 13-12. It was their first game since March 5 ne year ago when the season was canceled after only four games due to Covid-19. The squad came into the night with just two weeks of full “This felt like a playoff game,” said head coach Carlton Chan. “I always say lacrosse is a great way to end the drought,’ he added, standing in the pouring rain but jubilant after a close win. “It was really nice to see the girls out here. For several of them it was their first varsity game,” he added. Tuesday’s game had all the makings of a late-season clash of powerhouse programs. In a typical Division 2 matchup in North Coast Section, the beating rain only added to the thrilling atmosphere. Last night, Tuesday, March 9, playing under the lights at Witter Field in a rainstorm, they beat North Coast Section rival Acalanes 13-12. It was their first game since March 5 ne year ago when the season was canceled after only four games due to Covid-19. The squad came into the night with just two weeks of full practice. “This felt like a playoff game,” said head coach Carlton Chan. “I always say lacrosse is a great way to end the drought,’ he added, standing in the pouring rain but jubilant after a close win. “It was really nice to see the girls out here. For several of them it was their first varsity game,” he added. Tuesday’s game had all the makings of a late-season clash of powerhouse programs. In a typical Division 2 matchup in North Coast Section, the beating rain only added to the thrilling atmosphere. articles.text: Soprano Carrie Hennessey (right) and pianist Jennifer Reason Festival Opera will open its 2021 season on March 28 with a concert by soprano Carrie Hennessey and pianist Jennifer Reason. Hennessey and Reason, both internationally renowned artists, will perform in honor of Women’s History Month in an event entitled “And Yet She Persisted: Women in Classical Music.” “And Yet she Persisted” will explore the world of female composers. Audience members can expect to hear music crafted by mezzo-soprano Pauline Viardot and composer Amy Beach. Grammy Award-Winning composer Libby Larsen wrote music to the text of letters written by the American frontierswoman Calamity Jane. Julia Seeholzer said that her “Portraits of Disquiet,” originally composed during the 2016 election, feels “more potent now in our present day.” Kendall A, who remains “off the grid” purposefully, offers a song that details the relationship between her and her parents. Kendall includes quotes directly from Dante’s Inferno in Italian. Barbara Strozzi’s Lagrime Mie, a baroque lament, is musically quoted in Seeholzer’s opening line. Soprano Hennessey and pianist Reason both bring their own unique energy to the recital stage. The series of piano and vocal recitals are produced in accordance with strict COVID-19 testing and safety measures as advised by the Center for Disease Control and the Alameda County Department of Public Health. articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Simone McIntosh joins the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco for a concert premiering this Friday, March 12 at 7:30 p.m. Titled Art of the Voice, the concert will also be available on Sunday, March 14 at 6 p.m. The program takes viewers on a journey from the dark and stormy into the sunrise. Be transported by Beethoven’s passionate String Quartet Op. 18 no. 4, the haunting melodies of Respighi’s Il Tramonto, and the gentle glow of Haydn’s Sunrise Quartet. McIntosh’s powerful and soulful voice, possessing a wide range, captivates audiences. She will encore with Nadia Boulanger’s tender and serene Cantique, in a world premiere arrangement for voice and string quartet. Back by popular demand, the concert will include a trivia segment entitled “The Secret Lives of Divas and Divos – stars of the Opera.” “We are dedicated to performing chamber music in intimate and personal ways,” explained violinist Natasha Makhijani, a founding member of CMS of SF. “We carefully curate an experience that captures the imagination with exceptional music, while sharing the complexities of the musicians’ lives and their creative process.” “For years we’ve wanted to do a project with voice where the lyricism and story of the text come first. Right now is the opportunity, when our online concerts have the visual flexibility to transport you into the story itself,” added co-founder Samsun van Loon, “This story is Shelley’s poem The Sunset, the eternal story of love, loss, and perseverance, set to music by Ottorino Respighi as Il Tramonto for mezzo-soprano and string quartet. Filling for violist Clio Tilton, who is on maternity leave, will be Ivo Bokulic. The concert will stream on-demand through Sunday, March 21. For tickets, click on https:// chambermusicsocietysf.org/digital-concerts.

articles.text: Ben Affleck portrays Jack Cunningham in The Way Back. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Way Back is a remarkably good film that takes a familiar trope and course corrects, resulting in an honest, well-acted film that is far more than a formulaic sports story. Actually, it’s an intense character study, resulting in one of Ben Affleck’s finest performances in what has been a storied career. His portrayal of Jack Cunningham, a middle-aged construction worker, is a perfect fit, delivered with a personal authenticity that abandons the movie star/matinee idol persona. He fully embraces a role about a man deeply wounded by a life experience, one so profound, so wrenching that his recovery is uncertain. To the filmmakers’ credit, the arc of the story is neither the familiar tale of a faltering high school basketball team, nor is it simply a search for personal redemption. Movie review by Chris Honoré Harriet attempts to capture the essence of the historical figure Harriet Tubman (also known in her early years as Araminta Ross or “Minty”). While this film is a respectful and laudatory view of Harriet it feels like there is more to this courageous woman. As we’re told, Harriet (Cynthia Ervio) escapes slavery from a plantation in Bucktown, Maryland. The year is 1849. She is hunted from almost the first moment she is discovered missing, her value measured in dollars. Chased to a bridge, with slave hunters, her master (Joe Allwyn), and hounds in pursuit she climbs over the railing and jumps into a raging river. It’s a decision that is not only life threatening but symbolic. Clearly she would rather die than return to the plantation and live as a slave. She makes what proves to be a remarkable 100-mile trek to Philadelphia where black people live free. However, not long after arriving, it is evident that she is tormented by the memories of those she left behind, including her husband John (Zackary Momoh) and so she decides to return to Maryland and lead her husband and family to freedom. Thus begins a series of missions, each high risk/high gain. She knows that if she is caught, she will be killed. Eventually she guides some 70 slaves to Philadelphia through what became known as the “Underground Railroad.” She eventually became one of its most valued “conductors.” Tubman is an iconic character and deserves her story told on the big screen. Hers is a narrative of remarkable bravery. But it is also a story of slavery, which was an institution of extraordinary cruelty and brutality. It’s from that reality that Harriet escaped, making it all the more remarkable that she chose to return to help other slaves find freedom. What Harriet fails to do is reveal the horrible price paid by people who were treated like chattel, hundreds of thousands held against their will, countless killed or worked to death. That is the missing contrast to Harriet’s courage and humanity as well as her fierce determination. We’re told this quality was later recognized when she was given the command of an armed expedition during the Civil War; something unheard of up to that point. Harriet does deliver a profile in courage. But it also suggests that there is more to this remarkable woman’s story that needs to be told. Harriet. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Way Back is a remarkably good film that takes a familiar trope and course corrects, resulting in an honest, well-acted film that is far more than a formulaic sports story. Actually, it’s an intense character study, resulting in one of Ben Affleck’s finest performances in what has been a storied career. His portrayal of Jack Cunningham, a middle-aged construction worker, is a perfect fit, delivered with a personal authenticity that abandons the movie star/matinee idol persona. He fully embraces a role about a man deeply wounded by a life experience, one so profound, so wrenching that his recovery is uncertain. To the filmmakers’ credit, the arc of the story is neither the familiar tale of a faltering high school basketball team, nor is it simply a search for personal redemption. Instead, Affleck slowly opens a window into his character, Jack. In one scene, before work, he stands in the shower drinking a beer while shampooing; later, he spikes his morning coffee while on the job. He is a big man, thick through the middle, covered perpetually with a sheen of sweat as if his body is trying to expel the The Way Back amount of alcohol he consumes. He finishes his day at a favorite bar, chugging shots. Jack is married, but separated. Though still loved by his wife, Angela (Janina Gavankar), she has given up trying to live with him. Jack is not walking through life, he’s staggering, and his self-imposed isolation is inviolable. And even when he receives a phone call from his long-ago alma mater, Bishop Hayes, offering him a job – he was a standout basketball star with exceptional promise – it is not clear that he will be able to find a fragment of sobriety to earn the moniker “coach.” And so when he accepts to take on this losing team, we assume that this will be his way back. It’s a movie we’ve seen countless times: a coach needing this moment and a group of high schoolers needing his leadership. The field of play is the crucible. It’s that place where character and tenacity and courage matter. But the story veers off in a very different direction. In Hoosiers, Gene Hackman, basketball coach, stands court center with his small town team that has earned a slot in the State championship playoffs. He then sets up a ladder and measures the distance from the rim of the basket to the floor, showing the much-intimidated players that it’s the same distance as their home court. Same rules, same ball, just a different court. He tells them to play their game. Which they do in spades. It’s wonderful. But The Way Back is not Hoosiers. There is only one way back and that is forward to a far different ending. One last comment about Ben Affleck. For years he has been tabloid fodder, going back to his near-miss engagement to Jennifer Lopez. To be a movie star can be a long walk on a high wire. The movie industry is replete with individuals who have succumbed to the promise of glamor and fame. Affleck’s personal journey has been painfully chronicled by the tabloid press, exposing his struggles with alcohol and gambling and a failed marriage to Jennifer Garner. Perhaps his commitment to capturing the essence of Jack Cunningham is just a precursor to what awaits him, not as a movie star but as an actor. To emerge with one’s self and integrity intact is truly remarkable. The Way Back. Directed by Gavin O’Connor. Starring Ben Affleck, Al Madrigal, and Janina Gavankar. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated R. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s The Jungle Book. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Jungle Book is a dazzling, vibrant film that will draw kids in and easily keep them in their seats. Starring Neel Sethi as Mowgli (the only human, also known as the “man cub”), the film is a marvel of CGI. A thought that comes to mind is that kids today may take for granted the seamless creation of animals, such as the bear Baloo (Bill Murray), or the panther, Bagheera (Ben Kingsley). For those of us who have watched movies over the years, the technical accomplishments of this film are nothing short of astonishing. Using the original Jungle Book story by Rudyard Kipling as the source material, Mowgli is confronted with a difficult choice. If he is to survive, he must leave his family of wolves and all that he has known and escape the lethal wrath of Shere Khan (Idris Elba), a tiger that hates men so much that he is intent on killing Mowgli. His journey takes him deep into the Indian jungle where he is confronted with one adventure after the next. It is there that he meets the lazy Baloo, who asks Mowgli to climb a steep cliff to get at the honey hives hanging from the rocks. He also falls under the spell of an enormous snake Kaa (Scarlett Johansson), and meets to his peril King Louie, a Gigantopithecus (Christopher Walken), from whom he barely escapes. Mowgli’s goal – the purpose of his adventure – is to find a place of human habitation in order to escape Shere Kahn. At his side is Bagheera, his wise and helpful mentor, who urges him on, for the panther knows that Mowgli’s life is in danger. Shere Kahn will never stop his relentless pursuit. Kids will lose themselves in this movie. It’s technologically breathtaking. But keep in mind that it can also be intense and may be a bit scary for youngsters under 8. There are moments when the animals confront each other and the outcome can be sad and final. The Jungle Book is a joy to watch; it is lush and energetic with scenes that are light-hearted and will make the kids smile. Enjoy. The Jungle Book. Directed by Jon Favreau. Starring Neel Sethi, Bill Murrray and Ben Kingsley. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The idea, which comprises the essence of Pixar’s Inside Out, is inspired. Written and directed by Piedmont resident Pete Docter in 2015, the film won an Academy Award as Best Animation Feature. Of significance, the filmmakers confronted the third dimension in movies (emotion). It is, after all, a world in which animators can take a step that otherwise would be impossible in a photographed feature. Knowing that a filmed narrative cannot penetrate a character’s mind (except by using a voiceover), they tell a familiar story of an 11-year-old girl named Riley (Kaitlyn Dias). She lives happily in the embrace of her parents in Minnesota, has loads of friends and plays on a hockey team. For Riley life is better than good. That is until her father takes a new job and they must relocate to San Francisco. Up to this point, Riley’s default setting is contentment and joy – school, friends, sports all fit into a much-enjoyed spectrum of childhood on the cusp of being a teenager (Riley defines the word tween). With the move across the country, Riley’s world is rocked. She is confronted with challenges that are new to her. Her new house is a bit grim, as is her neighborhood. She tries out for hockey and it doesn’t go well. Suddenly Riley begins to slide into a funk. And though her parents ask her if everything is all right (of course, Riley grumbles that all is fine), the emotions taking place inside are a different story. The Pixar storytellers craft a kind of emotional wheelhouse (in Riley’s head, so to speak) and personify all of Riley’s emotions. It’s wonderful. There’s Joy (Amy Poehler), Fear (Bill Hader), Anger (Lewis Black), Disgust (Mindy Kaling) and Sadness (Phyllis Smith). Each emotion is a unique and funny and engaging character, and all coping with Riley’s new world and a bevy of feelings that are at first decidedly unsettling. Riley has always been encouraged to be happy. To smile. But then she has been grounded in a spiffy life. Hence Joy, vivacious and energetic, has always had her hand on the tiller, suddenly Anger and Fear and Sadness (most especially) find that their roles in Riley’s emotions are growing. Meanwhile, Joy, becomes lost in a labyrinth of Riley’s mind and must struggle to find its way back to emotion central before things get really awful for Riley. You have to see the crew in action (Anger is a squat, red, short-fused guy) to get a complete understanding of what Pixar has accomplished as it tells a compelling story, one that kids will relate to and one that adults will quickly recognize. Growth is dealing with the internal dialogue/monologue that takes place all of our lives. This may be Riley’s first experience with an unfamiliar spectrum of emotions, but it won’t be her last. And beginning on the journey of dealing with the crew up in the wheelhouse, to include Sadness and Fear and Anger, as well as Joy, she must make choices and sort stuff out. Of course, it’s all a central if imperfect part of life. It’s also the meaning of “growing up” (a lifelong process). Which Riley eventually comes to realize. Watch for the credits. They’re terrific. As is Inside Out. Inside Out. Directed by Pete Docter. Animated from Pixar Animation Studios and Walt Disney Pictures. 1 hr., 34 min. Rated PG A scene from Pixar’s Inside Out.

The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its Zoom book discussion on March 1. Thirteen readers were on the call to discuss their March selection, Drive Your Plow over the Bones of the Dead, by Polish author Olga Tokarczuk. Participating were Mike Bandrowski, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Sally Arney, Albert Chen, Karin Fetherston, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The group was also pleased to welcome first-time participant Jamie Forsythe, a long-time, childhood friend on Priscilla Wanerus. Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead is Tokarczuk’s 2009 mystery novel. The book’s title is from a William Blake poem, “Proverbs of Hell,” which contains the line, “In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy. Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead.” The book was originally published in Polish and later translated to English by Antonia LloydJones. The novel received a wide release in 2019 when it was published in the United States. It received strong, poitive reviews, and Tokarczuk was awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Literature for her writings, two months after the novel’s U.S. release. Lloyd-Jones’ translation was also acclaimed and received awards. Piedmont readers agreed on March 1 that the book was excellent. Tokarczuk’s protagonist is Janina, an aging astrologist who lives in a secluded Polish village on the Czech border. She spends her time pontificating on broad concepts, translating the poetry of Blake, and predicting people’s futures through her sophisticated astrology. However, there is friction between Janina and her neighbors who are hunters; it is a conflict that drives the entire novel. For Janina, the killing of innocent creatures is murder. Everyone in her village thinks Janina is more than eccentric, and maybe a little crazy. Janina is certainly a character. However, as the novel progresses there seems to be reason to believe that she’s right in thinking that the dead bodies turning up all around her are acts of revenge on the local hunters by animals. The storyline takes the reader through a number of murders in the village to the ultimate solution of them, and a happy ending of sorts. Almost all the members of the group enjoyed the book. articles.text: Schools are opening…finally. This is an open letter to parents and students. Studying music offers many wonderful opportunities. Some of the things that music does approaches miracle status. Here is a case in point. Many years ago, I played a concert in a senior residence home. After the concert, one of the residents came up to me and engaged me in conversation. She told me about her honeymoon some 50 years earlier. She and her husband went to Norway. As she continued to reminisce, she described going to the Ole Bull museum outside Bergen. For those of you who do not recognize the name, Ole Bull was Norway’s greatest violinist and also contributed greatly to American culture. There’s even a song about him and the Utopian society he sought to create: “Oleana”. The woman’s description of her honeymoon was vivid in every detail. She even described seeing Ole Bull’s violin which had a man’s head sculpted at the top. I enjoyed my conversation with her very much. When she departed for dinner, the nurse came up with the most astonished look I have ever seen on a person’s face. The nurse told me that this lady had severe and profound dementia, and she hadn’t spoken a word in months. My music stirred her in a miraculous way. That is only one reason for music. But students at all ages should have the opportunity to learn and appreciate music. The easiest thing to do is to take a music appreciation class. I do not know if Piedmont Middle School or the high school offer music appreciation classes. For more than 25 years Joe Piazza, and before him Alan Harvey taught music theory and music appreciation classes at Piedmont High, classes that proved to be popular year after year. Psychological tests have proved that simply listening to music increases the intelligence and does good things for the spirit. Playing music is even better because it is a participation sport. You will learn another language. At the same time, you learn to work together as a team as well as improve personal discipline. It’s always a good idea to remember that participation in music is fun. You learn problem-solving in enjoyable ways. There is also the social aspect. That was what kept my son involved in music. He enjoyed himself so thoroughly that he decided to make music his life. Musicians lead exciting lives. We have friends everywhere in the world and have the opportunity to travel extensively and visit and perform with them. One other thing to consider is that audiences love what musicians do. It isn’t just the applause; audience members Virtuoso Norwegian violinist and composer Ole Bull. will come to the stage and want to speak to the performers. If that isn’t gratification, I don’t know what is. So many of the great musicians were also great role models. So… Let me mention two of them. One is Ezzard Charles. His nickname was the “Cincinnati Cobra”. To those who know about boxing, Ezzard Charles was one of the great boxers of all time and the Heavyweight champ of the world. A Black man, he grew up in the segregated south. But he valued education. During World War II he was stationed in Italy. He came back speaking Italian. There is a beautiful news clip in which he is speaking in Italian with his nemesis, Rocky Marciano. For two great rivals, this was a perfect example of respect and friendship. A less publicized part of his life was the fact that Ezzard Charles played the cello. Another good example is a friend from Oklahoma City. Virginia Campbell was laid to rest just a few days ago at the age of 88. Her story is extraordinary. She married at a young age and had four children. After the four children got married and left the house, Virginia got a college degree in music, with a major in piano performance. Rather than embark on a playing career, she became the most important impresario in Oklahoma City. For 35 years she presented concerts of international quality. She got a church to donate its facilities as a concert hall, with all post-concert receptions catered. All concert artists were of international quality. Virginia was chosen as Miss Senior Oklahoma and was a finalist in the Miss Senior USA “beauty-talent“ competitions. She did perform and traveled throughout the world giving concerts and teaching. Consider all of the things she did, and then know that Virginia Campbell was legally blind. Studying music is all for the good. Do it because it makes you smarter. Do it for all the reasons above but, remember that playing music is lots of fun. The opportunities are there. Remember the adage: when opportunity knocks, it’s a good idea to open the door.

Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead.” The book was originally published in Polish and later translated to English by Antonia LloydJones. The novel received a wide release in 2019 when it was published in the United States. It received strong, poitive reviews, and Tokarczuk was awarded the 2018 Nobel Prize in Literature for her writings, two months after the novel’s U.S. release. Lloyd-Jones’ translation was also acclaimed and received awards. Piedmont readers agreed on March 1 that the book was excellent. Tokarczuk’s protagonist is Janina, an aging astrologist who lives in a secluded Polish village on the Czech border. She spends her time pontificating on broad concepts, translating the poetry of Blake, and predicting people’s futures through her sophisticated astrology. However, there is friction between Janina and her neighbors who are hunters; it is a conflict that drives the entire novel. For Janina, the killing of innocent creatures is murder. Everyone in her village thinks Janina is more than eccentric, and maybe a little crazy. Janina is certainly a character. However, as the novel progresses there seems to be reason to believe that she’s right in thinking that the dead bodies turning up all around her are acts of revenge on the local hunters by animals. The storyline takes the reader through a number of murders in the village to the ultimate solution of them, and a happy ending of sorts. Almost all the members of the group enjoyed the book. The popularity of this style in the early 1900’s was to a large degree an alternative to the modThe Tudor style is characterized by steeply pitched, front facing gable roofs. There are, however, frequent variations and exceptions in this “playful” style of architecture with hipped roofs sometimes used in conjunction with the gables. ernism that was being developed in Europe with machined components and lack of ornamentation. People wanted a more handcrafted feeling that ended up being expressed in Tudor homes. As a matter of fact, the Tudor style was closely associated with the Arts and Crafts movement which was being developed at the same time for many of the same reasons. I often wonder why a certain architectural style becomes popular and then remains so for so many years. I think that certainly one reason is because these styles were well developed over a long period of time. Proportions, material selections, and detailing conventions were worked out over the years on different buildings until they became….fine architecture! Certainly. this was the case on the cathedrals that took hundreds of years to build. After building a part of it, seeing it for a few years or even decades, the sponsors and architects were able to re-design and correct functional and aesthetic components, sometimes even changing the architectural style completely. In any case, the Tudor style developed into an appealing and desirable architecture all over this country. The visual giveaway of course is the half-timbered walls, consisting of a squared heavy timber frame structural system originally infilled with masonry or a stucco like mixture know as wattle between the timbers. My world has been a beehive of activity for days — shopping and curating. Honestly, getting everything together for the reveal, styling the space, this final pulling together of art and objects is so satisfying. But also it’s hard work, with much angst, hunger (emotional and physical), and running around from vendor to vendor. Still, I have grown to love all of it. Which is not to say I’m only shopping in the final days before a photo shoot. For example, styling our most recent project started a month ago. My studio director (a.k.a. work A few finds from a day on the coast: birds, books, lamp. wife) Darshan and I were having a girls’ weekend, staying at a client’s vacation house on the coast. One day we headed out in search of lunch and a view of the ocean and we ended up finding this fantastic vintage store. We were there for over two hours wandering through a place so full of treasures. The owner stayed late with us and we had such fun picking through her wares, thinking about our different projects — shopping and mentally curating. We found a gorgeous mid-century lamp with a black carved-wood sculptural base. We brought it last week to its place of destiny – a client’s entry console table (see the photo). I love to decorate with antique books. At this same shop we found a pristine three-volume dictionary in a rich dark blue, and a set of the collected works of Edgar Allan Poe, several small volumes bound in red. What we look for when we are styling bookcases is not just books but also objects to display on the shelves. A set of carved birds, a small antique desk globe, a mid-century ashtray with a horse motif (that will go to our client who smokes cigars); a very large crystal cluster that will be perfect for another client’s powder room vanity. It is now an experience of beauty that is transcendent. It’s the feeling that happens when a room comes to life — that is the addictive transformation that keeps me in this business, happily, over all of these years. articles.text: Stephen Edward Block, age 84, died peacefully in his sleep on January 18, 2021, with Dale, his wife of fifty years, by his side. Stephen was a life-long East Bay resident and a long time East Bay real estate developer. Born Stephen Edward Block in Oakland on March 16, 1936, he was the son of George and Gladys Block. He attended Crocker Highlands Elementary and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1954. He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Civil Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1958, While at Cal Stephen joined his older brother George as a member of the Zeta Beta Tau fraternity and was also a member of the U.S. Army Reserve Officer Training Corps. After graduation, he served as an officer in the Army’s Counterintelligence Corps. Blessed with an impish sense of humor, while in the Army he was known for using the Presidio parade ground as a driving range. In 1970, Stephen married Dale Block (née Forrest), and in 1972 they welcomed their only son Adam. As his family grew, Stephen invested his energies in his real estate business as well. Over the years he developed a range of office, industrial, and residential projects, including Moraga Country Club, Kelton Court, and a variety of build-to-suit warehouses. Piedmont alums Clark Wallace and Bob Goetz, along with Block were the brains and brawn behind the Moraga Country Club project in 1971. (One phone has since been recovered.) Ware was seen running on foot on Arbor Drive and getting in the passenger side of a white Lexus RX300. Ware and the accomplice fled the city, but an automated license plate reader captured the license plate number. A detailed description of the individual and the gun was given to the police by the robbery victim. This information was shared with other local law enforcement agencies. Two weeks later, at 1:00pm on July 25, 2020, Ware robbed another victim, a 43-year-old woman in the parking lot of a grocery store in San Lorenzo. He ran up behind the woman as she was attempting to get in her car, knocked her to the ground, and ripped her purse from her arm. In a coordinated effort by Piedmont and Oakland police officers, Ware was arrested for both crimes six days later on July 31, 2020. On February 18, 2021 a jury convicted Ware of second-degree robbery with personal use of a firearm, an additional second degree robbery, identity theft, possession of a firearm as a convicted felon, and several other firearms and ammunition offenses. Background to an investigation On July 31, 2020, the day of his arrest, Oakland Police officers noticed Ware on Douglas Avenue in Oakland. They observed him get into the driver’s seat of his white Lexus RX300 and detained him before he could drive away. Officers found an unregistered and loaded black Smith & Wesson .45 caliber handgun next to the driver’s seat. The handgun had multiple distinctive markings on it consistent with the detailed description provided by the Piedmont victim. “What really cracked [the case] was that her credit card was used at [the] Target [store] in San Leandro. We were able to get video surveillance and it matched up with surveillance we had in Piedmont,” explained Piedmont Detective Jeff Spranza. Investigative efforts by Spranza and Piedmont Det. John Lagios confirmed Ware as the suspect. “At the time [of the crime] the car was not registered in his name. Through investigation we learned that he purchased that vehicle in February 2020. Her case is pending. Ware remains in Santa Rita Jail on a no-bail hold and has a sentencing date of March 18. He could be given a term of 18 or more years in prison. “With this investigation we were able to identify two suspects and brought closure to the victim and the residents of Piedmont. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) isolated the break within an hour after it occurred. “When I visited the site about 30 minutes after the break occurred, EBMUD was onsite, and the break was isolated when the surrounding water valves were shut off. Fortunately, EBMUD was able to isolate the break and keep water service on for residents in the surrounding area, so we didn’t have any reports of water service being interrupted,” Gonzales said. Oakland Avenue – a main thoroughfare and a bus route – was closed off on Monday between San Carlos Ave. and Carmel Ave. while repairs were made.
